concepts.title: Principles of Biotechnology: Genetic Engineering and Bioprocesses
concepts.definition: Biotechnology uses living organisms or their enzymes to make products and processes people need -- curd and wine in the old sense, genetically modified organisms at scale in the modern sense; its two core techniques are genetic engineering, which rewrites the chemistry of dna or rna and installs it in a host to change the host's phenotype, and bioprocess engineering, which keeps a sterile, contamination-free environment so only the chosen cells multiply for making antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes.
concepts.key_idea: Traditional hybridisation drags undesirable genes along with wanted ones -- recombinant dna, gene cloning and gene transfer let you carry only the desired gene across.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 49-125 (EFB definition, two core techniques, hybridisation limitation, ori and cloning idea)
question_patterns: define biotechnology in both its traditional and modern senses
name the two core techniques that gave rise to modern biotechnology
what does bioprocess engineering maintain and why does sterility matter
why is sexual reproduction's variation an advantage for breeders
why must alien dna be linked to an origin of replication to multiply in a host
how does genetic engineering avoid carrying undesirable genes across

solution_steps.action: Take the wide and narrow views
solution_steps.explain: Microbe-made curd, bread and wine qualify broadly; today the word usually means processes using genetically modified organisms, plus in vitro fertilisation, gene synthesis, dna vaccines and gene correction.
Genetic engineering alters genetic-material chemistry and moves it into hosts; bioprocess engineering keeps sterile conditions so only the wanted microbe or eukaryotic cell grows in bulk.

solution_steps.action: See why cloning needs an ori
solution_steps.explain: A loose dna fragment cannot multiply in a new cell; hitched to a chromosome's origin of replication -- or to a vector carrying one -- it replicates and is inherited, giving multiple identical copies.
Cohen and boyer linked an antibiotic-resistance gene to a salmonella plasmid with restriction enzymes and ligase, transferred it into e. coli, and multiplied the gene -- the first recombinant dna.

concepts.title: Three Basic Steps of Genetically Modifying an Organism
concepts.definition: Every genetic-modification project runs the same three-step play: identify the dna carrying the desirable gene, introduce that dna into the host, and keep it maintained there so it passes to the host's progeny; each stage has its own toolkit, from restriction cutting and ligation through vector delivery to selection of transformed cells.
concepts.key_idea: Identify, introduce, maintain -- the entire chapter is these three verbs elaborated with enzymes, vectors and hosts.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 153-161 (the three basic steps) and 420-427 (process sequence)
question_patterns: list the three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism
what must be done after the desirable gene is introduced into the host
in what sequence do the processes of recombinant dna technology run
why must introduced dna be transferred to the progeny of the host
how is the dna with desirable genes identified before transfer
which step of genetic modification uses vectors and which uses selection

solution_steps.explain: The dna fragment bearing desirable genes is cut out of its source with restriction endonucleases and separated on a gel.
The fragment is ligated into a vector and the recombinant dna is delivered into a competent host cell by transformation, micro-injection, gene gun or disarmed pathogen.
An origin of replication lets the construct multiply in the host, selectable markers let only transformed cells survive, and the dna must reach the progeny for the change to stick.

concepts.title: Restriction Enzymes: Palindromes and Sticky Ends
concepts.definition: Restriction endonucleases are the molecular scissors of genetic engineering -- hind ii was the first found to cut one specific six-base-pair recognition sequence, and over 900 such enzymes now come from more than 230 bacterial strains; each scans for a palindromic site that reads identically on both strands in the 5'-to-3' direction and cuts a little off-centre, leaving overhanging sticky ends that hydrogen-bond to their complements and invite dna ligase to seal the joint.
concepts.key_idea: Cut vector and insert with the same enzyme and their sticky ends match -- that single rule makes recombinant dna construction reproducible.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 168-231 (Hind II, EcoRI naming, nucleases, palindrome GAATTC, sticky ends, recombinant formation)
question_patterns: how are restriction enzymes named and what does ecori stand for
differentiate exonucleases from endonucleases
what is a palindromic sequence in dna and give an example
how do sticky ends help in forming recombinant dna
why must the vector and the source dna be cut by the same restriction enzyme
which was the first restriction endonuclease characterised and how long is its recognition sequence

solution_steps.explain: Two e. coli enzymes from 1963 started the story -- one methylated dna, one cut it; hind ii came five years later. Names encode source: eco ri reads escherichia coli strain ry 13, with roman numerals for order of isolation.
Exonucleases nibble nucleotides from dna ends; endonucleases cut at specific positions inside the molecule.

Each enzyme inspects the dna until it finds its palindromic recognition site -- gaattc on one strand pairing cttaag on the other -- and cuts both backbones slightly off centre, between the same two bases.
The single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends) pair by hydrogen bonding with complementary cut ends, and dna ligase permanently joins them -- fragments cut by the same enzyme fit end-to-end.

concepts.title: Gel Electrophoresis and Elution of DNA Fragments
concepts.definition: Because dna carries negative charge, an electric field drags restriction fragments through an agarose gel toward the anode, and the gel's sieve effect sorts them by size -- the smallest travel farthest; staining with ethidium bromide and viewing under uv light reveals bright orange bands, which are then cut out of the gel and eluted for use in constructing recombinant dna.
concepts.key_idea: Size decides the distance -- the gel is a molecular sieve, and the sample well must sit at the cathode end so fragments run toward the anode.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 242-269 (electrophoresis principle, agarose, ethidium bromide, UV, elution)
question_patterns: why do dna fragments move toward the anode during electrophoresis
how does an agarose gel separate dna fragments of different sizes
why cannot dna bands be seen without staining
which stain is used to visualise dna in a gel
what is elution and when is it performed
at which end of the gel is the sample loaded and why

solution_steps.explain: Negatively charged dna fragments migrate toward the anode through the agarose matrix under the electric field.
The gel's mesh resists large fragments more, so fragments resolve strictly by size -- smaller ones run farther from the loading well.
Ethidium bromide staining followed by uv exposure lights the bands bright orange; unstained dna is invisible in ordinary light.
Each band is sliced out of the gel and the dna extracted from the gel piece -- elution -- yielding pure fragments ready for ligation into cloning vectors.

concepts.title: Cloning Vectors: ori, Selectable Marker and Cloning Sites
concepts.definition: A cloning vector -- plasmid or bacteriophage dna that replicates autonomously in bacteria -- needs three essentials: an origin of replication that also sets the copy number, a selectable marker such as antibiotic-resistance genes that lets transformants outgrow non-transformants, and very few (ideally single) recognition sites for ligating alien dna; in pbr322 inserting at the bamh i site of the tetracycline gene knocks that resistance out, and chromogenic-substrate systems flag recombinants by losing colour through insertional inactivation of beta-galactosidase.
concepts.key_idea: One resistance gene selects transformants, the other reports the insert -- two antibiotic plates, or one colour test, settle which colonies are recombinant.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 270-371 (copy numbers, ori, selectable markers, pBR322 BamHI/tetR, insertional inactivation)
question_patterns: list the features required of a good cloning vector
why must a cloning vector carry an origin of replication and what else does the ori control
why do vectors need a selectable marker
in pbr322 how do you tell a recombinant colony from a non recombinant one
what is insertional inactivation and how does it show up on a plate
why should a vector carry only one recognition site for a restriction enzyme

solution_steps.explain: Any dna tied to the origin of replication replicates inside the host; picking a high-copy ori multiplies the target dna many-fold -- plasmids range from one or two up to 15-100 copies per cell, phages higher still.
Transformation is inefficient, so genes for ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin resistance mark which cells actually took the vector.
Multiple recognition sites would shred the vector; a single site -- e.g. bamh i inside pbr322's tetracycline-resistance gene -- takes the insert cleanly.

Recombinants keep ampicillin resistance but lose tetracycline resistance (insertion disrupts tet r), so they grow on ampicillin plates but not tetracycline; colour systems simplify this -- an insert knocking out beta-galactosidase leaves colonies colourless on chromogenic substrate while non-recombinants turn blue.

concepts.title: Vectors for Plants and Animals: Ti Plasmid and Retroviruses
concepts.definition: Nature's own gene-deliverers became biotech's vectors: agrobacterium tumifaciens naturally injects t-dna into dicot plant cells to make tumors, so its tumor-inducing (ti) plasmid was disarmed into a harmless delivery vehicle for genes of interest, and retroviruses, which normally transform animal cells cancerous, were similarly neutered to ferry desirable genes into animal cells.
concepts.key_idea: Disarm the pathogen, keep the delivery machinery -- the trick that converted plant tumors and animal cancers into genetic-engineering tools.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 373-393 (Agrobacterium T-DNA, Ti plasmid modified, retroviruses disarmed)
question_patterns: how does agrobacterium tumifaciens naturally transform plant cells
what is t dna and what does it do in infected plants
how was the ti plasmid converted into a safe cloning vector
why are retroviruses useful vectors for animal cells
what does disarming a pathogen vector mean
which natural pathogens taught scientists gene delivery to eukaryotes

solution_steps.explain: Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a dicot pathogen, delivers a dna piece (t-dna) that turns normal plant cells into tumors producing the pathogen's chemicals; retroviruses do the equivalent to animal cells.
The ti plasmid was modified so it no longer causes tumors yet still delivers -- now it carries genes of our choosing into many plants.

Retroviruses, stripped of their harmful transformations, deliver desirable genes into animal cells; once ligated into any suitable vector the construct is transferred into bacterial, plant or animal hosts to multiply.

concepts.title: Making the Host Competent and Routes of DNA Entry
concepts.definition: Hydrophilic dna cannot cross a cell membrane on its own, so bacteria are made competent by soaking them in a divalent cation such as calcium, which widens efficiency through wall pores; recombinant dna then goes in with an ice-42 degree-ice heat shock, while animal cells can receive dna by micro-injection into the nucleus, plant cells by gene-gun bombardment with gold or tungsten microparticles, and both by disarmed-pathogen vectors that infect and deliver.
concepts.key_idea: Four delivery routes, one goal -- get dna through a membrane that chemistry says it cannot cross.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 394-417 (calcium competence, heat shock, micro-injection, biolistics/gene gun, disarmed pathogens)
question_patterns: why must bacterial cells be made competent before taking up dna
what role do calcium ions play in bacterial transformation
describe the ice heat shock ice procedure for introducing dna
how does a gene gun deliver dna into plant cells
what is micro injection and which cells suit it best
how do disarmed pathogen vectors introduce recombinant dna

solution_steps.explain: Dna is hydrophilic and blocked by membranes; treating cells with a specific concentration of a divalent cation like calcium boosts dna entry through pores in the wall.
Cells incubated with recombinant dna on ice are given a brief 42-degree heat shock and returned to ice -- the pulse lets the plasmid slip in.

Micro-injection shoots dna straight into an animal cell's nucleus; biolistics (gene gun) fires dna-coated gold or tungsten microparticles into plant cells; disarmed pathogens infect and deliver their cargo.

concepts.title: Isolating and Cutting the Genetic Material
concepts.definition: Pure dna is the starting material, so cells are burst open with lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells and chitinase for fungi; ribonuclease strips rna, protease removes proteins such as histones, and chilled ethanol precipitates the cleaned dna as fine spoolable threads, after which restriction digestion -- checked on an agarose gel -- cuts both the source dna and the vector at matching sites for ligation.
concepts.key_idea: Each contaminant has its own enzyme -- rna for ribonuclease, protein for protease, cell walls for lysozyme, cellulase or chitinase -- leaving dna alone.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 428-464 (enzyme lysis, RNase, protease, chilled ethanol spooling, digestion and gel check)
question_patterns: which enzymes break open bacterial plant and fungal cells for dna isolation
how are rna and proteins removed from a crude dna extract
why is chilled ethanol added at the end of dna purification
why must dna be pure before restriction digestion
how do you monitor the progress of a restriction enzyme digestion
what happens after both the source dna and the vector are cut

solution_steps.explain: Bacterial cells yield to lysozyme, plant cells to cellulase, fungal cells to chitinase -- releasing dna together with rna, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids.
Ribonuclease degrades rna and protease digests the histone-associated proteins; other impurities fall to suitable treatments.
Adding chilled ethanol pulls the purified dna out as a visible tangle of fine threads that can be spooled off.

Purified dna and vector are incubated separately with the chosen restriction enzyme under its optimal conditions, agarose gel electrophoresis confirms the digestion, and ligase then joins gene of interest to opened vector -- recombinant dna.

concepts.title: PCR Amplification of the Gene of Interest
concepts.definition: The polymerase chain reaction synthesises multiple copies of a chosen dna segment in vitro using two primer sets -- short synthetic oligonucleotides complementary to the target's flanks -- plus a dna polymerase; every cycle of denaturation, primer annealing and extension doubles the copies, and the thermostable polymerase from thermus aquaticus survives the heat that separates the strands, so about thirty cycles build roughly a billion-fold amplification.
concepts.key_idea: Doubling per cycle is the whole arithmetic -- a thermostable polymerase is what lets the doubling repeat dozens of times without fresh enzyme.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 465-486 (PCR steps, primers, Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, billion copies)
question_patterns: what are the three steps of each pcr cycle
why is a thermostable dna polymerase needed in pcr
from which bacterium was the heat stable polymerase of pcr isolated
work out how many copies of a dna segment remain after a given number of pcr cycles
what role do primers play in the polymerase chain reaction
roughly how many copies does pcr produce after about thirty cycles

solution_steps.explain: Each cycle -- denaturation, primer annealing, extension of primers -- doubles the number of target copies.

concepts.title: Bioreactors and Downstream Processing
concepts.definition: Transformed hosts are grown at scale in stirred-tank bioreactors handling 100-1000 litres, equipped with agitators, oxygen delivery, foam, temperature and ph controls and sampling ports so cells stay in their most productive exponential phase; afterwards downstream processing separates and purifies the product, formulates it with preservatives and puts it through clinical trials and strict quality control before marketing.
concepts.key_idea: A small flask culture never yields useful quantities -- scale-up in a bioreactor, then purification and quality control, turn a cloned gene into a sellable product.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo109.txt lines 487-603 (selection on ampicillin, recombinant protein, continuous culture, stirred-tank bioreactor, downstream processing)
question_patterns: what capacities and controls does a stirred tank bioreactor offer
why does a small scale laboratory culture give poor product yields
what is a recombinant protein and where is it expressed
how does a continuous culture system keep cells in exponential phase
list the processes included in downstream processing
why must the finished biotech product undergo clinical trials and quality control

solution_steps.explain: Spreading cells on ampicillin plates keeps only those carrying the resistance-gene construct -- the selectable marker at work; the alien dna must then be expressed under tuned conditions.

Continuous culture drains spent medium while feeding fresh, holding cells at peak physiology; bioreactors of 100-1000 litres with stirrers, sparged air, and foam, temperature, ph controls provide optimal growth conditions.
Downstream processing extracts the protein from the biomass and applies separation and purification techniques.
The product is formulated with preservatives, run through clinical trials as drugs are, and released only after strict quality-control testing tailored to each product.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo109.txt lines 465-486 (PCR doubling per cycle and billion copies)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A pcr run completes {cycles} cycles starting from one copy of the target segment. Roughly how many copies of the segment exist at the end?

solution_template.explain: Every cycle of denaturation, annealing and extension doubles the copies, so the count is two raised to the cycle number: two to the thirtieth, about a billion.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo109.txt lines 324-357 (pBR322 BamHI insert and two-plate selection)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Foreign dna was ligated into the bamh i site inside the tetracycline resistance gene of vector pbr322, and e coli was transformed. Sort the colonies: which grow on ampicillin, which on tetracycline, and which are recombinant?

solution_template.explain: Inserting dna at bamh i breaks the tetracycline-resistance gene, so recombinant plasmids keep ampicillin resistance but lose tetracycline resistance.
Recombinants grow on ampicillin medium but fail on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both -- transformants are chosen on ampicillin, then recombinants identified by tetracycline sensitivity.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo109.txt lines 181-190 (naming convention for restriction enzymes)
worked_examples.question_pattern: The restriction enzyme {enzyme_name} was isolated from a bacterium. Decode its name into genus, species, strain and order of discovery.

solution_template.explain: The first letter e comes from escherichia and the next two letters co from coli -- the source organism's binomial.
The capital r denotes the strain ry 13, and the roman numeral i marks it as the first enzyme isolated from that strain.
